summary: This unit teaches you to get a conduit wiring job ready before any conduit is fixed. You will learn to read the work order, drawings and specification, survey the site and plan the route, control the hazards and isolate existing circuits safely, and choose and check the conduit, fittings, cable, tools and access equipment. You will also work out a materials list, mark out the route, work with other trades, keep the site tidy and report that the job is ready.

blocks.p: Before a single length of conduit is fixed, someone has to read the drawings, walk the building, sort out clashes with other trades, make the site safe, get the right materials and tools, and mark the route on the walls. That is this unit. It is for Level 2 trainees who prepare conduit and wiring jobs under supervision. Good preparation makes the installation faster, neater and safer. Poor preparation shows up later as boxes at the wrong height, conduit that clashes with pipes, cables that cannot be pulled in and materials that run out halfway through the job.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Read work instructions and drawings
Read the work order, layout drawing, legend, scale, title block, revision and specification, and find each point on site.
Survey the site and plan the route
Walk the route with the drawing, find obstacles and hidden services, and plan a neat route with pull points where the cables will need them.
Identify hazards and control them
Take part in a risk assessment covering live circuits, work at height, dust and noise, hidden services, asbestos, overhead lines, trips and lifting.
Isolate existing circuits safely
Warn the people affected, then switch off, lock off, tag and prove dead before any work on or near existing wiring.
Choose and check PPE, tools and access equipment
Wear the right PPE for each task; check hand tools, power tools and ladders, and take faulty ones out of use.
Select and check materials
Choose the conduit, fittings, boxes, fixings and cable that the drawing and specification call for, and check them for type, size, rating and damage.
Work out quantities
Measure runs from the drawing, convert them with the scale, and write a materials list (take-off), rounding up and allowing for waste.
Mark out the route
Set box positions and heights from a datum, mark level and plumb lines, bends, boxes and saddle positions, and have the marking checked.
Work with others
Agree routes and timing with your supervisor, the customer and other trades, and report problems with the drawing.
Keep the site tidy and report
Store materials properly, clear waste, record route changes for the as-built drawing and report that the job is ready to start.

blocks.h: Where this unit fits in Jamaica

ul: Most Jamaican buildings are built of **reinforced concrete and hollow concrete block**. Much conduit is laid on the steel before a slab is poured, or run in the block cores and in chases as the walls go up. So preparation often happens on a live building site, alongside masons, steel fixers, plumbers and carpenters.

In finished buildings, such as offices, schools, clinics and shops, conduit is often run on the surface, and people go on using the building while you work. Then the occupants and the existing live wiring become part of your planning.

Homes and most small businesses are supplied at **110 V and 220 V, single-phase, 50 Hz**. Lighting and ordinary outlets are usually 110 V; water heaters, cookers, air-conditioners and pumps are often 220 V.

The electrical code used in Jamaica is based on the US **National Electrical Code (NEC)**. That is why you will meet US trade sizes for conduit (1/2 inch, 3/4 inch), wire sizes in AWG, and US words such as 'ground' and 'pull box', alongside British words such as 'earth' and 'draw-in box'. This kit gives both.
A new or altered installation must be inspected and certified before JPS will connect it. Preparation done carefully, to the drawing and the code, is the first step towards passing that inspection.

blocks.note: Preparation is real work, not a delay before the real work. An hour spent checking the drawing against the site can save a day spent taking out conduit that is in the wrong place.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow the job from the work order to the report at the end of the preparation stage. Then try the practice test and read every explanation, even for the questions you get right. Your instructor will show you the Centre's own forms, tools and materials.
Everything you prepare comes from the job's documents. Read them **before** you buy, cut or mark anything, and keep them with you on site.

head: Document
What it tells you
rows: Work order (job card)
What the job is, where, for whom, when, and who your supervisor is. It may list special conditions, such as working hours in a building that stays open.
Layout drawing (floor plan)
Where each light, switch, outlet, fan, panel and box goes, and often the conduit routes, drawn to scale as if you are looking down from above.
Elevation or section
A view of one wall, or a cut through the building, showing heights: switches, outlets, beams and the ceiling.
Wiring or schematic diagram
How the circuits are connected, which points are on which circuit, and the cable sizes.
Specification (the 'spec')
The type and quality of materials (for example 'rigid PVC conduit, 3/4 inch minimum'), the standard of work, the code to follow and the tests to be done.
Schedules
Lists, such as the panel schedule of circuits or a schedule of light fittings.
Maker's instructions
How a product must be installed: fixing spacings, bending limits, solvent cement drying times.

head: Part
What to look for
rows: Title block
Usually in the bottom right corner: the project name, drawing title and number, scale, who drew and checked it, and the date.
Legend (key)
What each symbol means. Symbols vary between designers, so always read the legend on **this** drawing.
Scale
How many times smaller the drawing is than the building, for example 1:50 or 1:100. A scale bar may also be drawn.
Revision box
The revision letter or number (A, B, C...), the date and what changed. Work only from the **latest revision**, and check that your copy matches the one in the site office.
Notes
Extra instructions, such as 'all conduit 3/4 inch unless noted' or 'outlet boxes 300 mm above FFL'.
Dimensions
Measurements written on the drawing. A written dimension is more reliable than a measurement taken off the paper.

blocks.p: Symbols differ from one drawing to another. These are typical on Jamaican drawings that follow US practice; the legend always has the final say.

head: Item
How it is often shown
rows: Ceiling light point
A circle, sometimes with a cross through it
Wall light
A circle or half-circle drawn against the wall line
Single-pole switch
The letter S
Three-way switch (British: two-way switch)
S3: two of these control one light from two places, such as each end of a passage
Duplex outlet, 110 V
A small circle with two short lines through it
Special outlet
The outlet symbol with letters or a note, such as 220V, GFI (GFCI protected) or WP (weatherproof)
Panelboard (distribution board)
A rectangle against the wall, often shaded
Circuit or conduit run

A line joining the points; an arrow towards the panel (a 'home run') marked with the circuit number. Solid, dashed or dotted lines may mean in the ceiling, in the floor or on the surface: read the legend.

blocks.p: A scale of **1:50** means 1 mm on the drawing is 50 mm on site. To change a drawing measurement into a real one, **multiply** by the scale number. To go the other way, divide.

head: Scale
1 mm on the drawing is
1 cm on the drawing is
Example
rows: 20 mm
45 mm on the drawing = 45 × 20 = 900 mm = 0.9 m
50 mm
72 mm on the drawing = 72 × 50 = 3,600 mm = 3.6 m
100 mm
38 mm on the drawing = 38 × 100 = 3,800 mm = 3.8 m

blocks.note: Use a **scale rule** set to the drawing's scale where you can, and always prefer a written dimension. Paper copies shrink or stretch when they are printed or photocopied, so a measurement taken off a copy can be out by several per cent. If a length looks wrong on site, check it with your supervisor.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: Before you start: check the documents

flow: Read the work order: what, where, when and who
Check that every drawing is the latest revision
Read the legend, the notes and the specification
Find each point on the drawing, then on site
List anything unclear, missing or wrong
Get answers from your supervisor before you buy, cut or fix

blocks.note: Never guess. If the drawing shows an outlet where a door now swings, a light under a beam or a route through a column, stop and ask. Changes are agreed with your supervisor and written on the drawing.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Surveying the site and planning the route

blocks.p: A drawing shows what the designer intended. The site shows what was actually built. Walk the whole route with the drawing in your hand, a tape measure and a notebook before you plan anything.

blocks.h: What to look for on the site survey

head: Look for
Why it matters
rows: The structure: block, concrete or drywall walls; beams, columns, slab thickness, ceiling type
It decides how conduit is fixed or buried, and where it can and cannot go. Never cut or drill a beam or column without the engineer's approval.
Obstacles: windows, doors and their swing, cupboards, air-conditioning units, water tanks, ducts
The route must go around them, and boxes must not end up behind a door or a cabinet.
Hidden services: cables, water and drain pipes, gas pipes in walls, floors and ceilings
Drilling into them can cause a shock, a flood or a gas leak. Check the drawings, ask the owner and scan with a detector.
The existing installation: panels, circuits and boxes
You may need to isolate circuits, and new work must not overload old circuits.
Access: ceiling height, ladder or platform needs, where materials can be stored
It decides the access equipment and how materials reach the work.
The environment: damp, sun, salt air, heat, places where conduit could be hit
It decides the type of conduit and fittings (see the materials section).
Hazards: possible asbestos, old wiring, overhead lines outside, open slab edges
Each one goes on the risk assessment.
Other trades and their work
Masons, plumbers, carpenters and air-conditioning fitters may want the same walls and ceilings.

blocks.h: Rules for a good conduit route

ul: Run conduit **straight, level and plumb**, parallel to walls, ceilings and the lines of the building. Diagonal runs on the surface look poor and are hard to work around later.

Use the **fewest bends** you can: every bend makes cables harder to pull in. Under the NEC a run between two pull points may have no more than the equivalent of **four quarter bends (360° in total)**.

Plan **draw-in (pull) boxes** on long runs and after several bends, so that cables can be pulled in without strain or damage, and replaced later. Pull boxes must stay **accessible**: never bury one behind plaster or a fixed ceiling.
Keep conduit away from hot surfaces, such as water heaters and the back of a stove, and away from water pipes where a leak could drip into a box.
Do not run conduit across a building's movement joint unless a fitting that allows movement is used.
Keep the route short, but not at the cost of neatness or safety.
Think ahead: leave spare conduits or space where the spec asks for future circuits.

blocks.note: Count the bends as you plan. A 90° bend, a 90° bend and an offset made of two 45° bends already add up to 270°. One more 90° bend reaches the 360° limit, so plan a pull box before the next bend.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Method
Where it is used
Planning points
rows: Cast in the slab
New concrete floors and roofs

Laid on the steel before the pour, tied down, joints sealed so wet concrete cannot get in, ends capped, boxes fixed to the formwork. It must be checked before the pour: mistakes found afterwards are very costly.
In block cores and chases
New and existing block walls
Run up the hollow cores as the wall is laid, or in chases cut later. Plan with the mason. Chases must not weaken the wall: follow the engineer's limits.
On the surface
Finished buildings, workshops, plant rooms
Fixed with saddles or straps. It must be straight and well supported; boxes and fittings are on show, so line them up.
Above a suspended ceiling
Offices, shops, schools
Supported from the building structure, not from the ceiling grid or its hanging wires.

blocks.p: Mark up a copy of the drawing as you go: measured lengths, obstacles, places where the route must change, and questions for your supervisor. Photographs help, as long as the owner agrees. This marked-up copy becomes the start of your materials list and of the **as-built** record.

sections.title: Hazards, risk assessment and safe isolation

blocks.p: Preparing for a conduit job looks like light work, but you will drill block, climb ladders, carry long lengths, work near existing circuits and sometimes find dangerous materials. Plan for each hazard before you start.

head: Hazard
What can happen
Control
rows: Existing live circuits near the work
Shock or burns when drilling, chasing or opening boxes
Find the circuits; isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead those you will work on or near. Treat all other wiring as live.
Hidden cables and pipes
Drilling into a live cable, a water pipe or a gas pipe
Check the drawings, ask the owner, scan with a cable and pipe detector, and drill with care to the marked depth.
Work at height
Falls from ladders, steps and slab edges
Sound fibreglass steps or a platform on firm, level ground; never stand on the top step; barriers at open slab edges.
Dust and noise from drilling and chasing
Eye injury, lung damage from fine concrete (silica) dust, hearing damage
Safety glasses, a dust mask (P2 or N95 class or better for chasing), ear protection; dust extraction or water where possible; keep others away.
Asbestos in older buildings
Fibres breathed in can cause deadly lung diseases many years later
Do not drill, cut or break it. Stop, keep people away and report it.
Overhead lines outside
A fatal shock if a length of conduit or a ladder touches a line
Look up; carry long items flat and low; keep well clear (at least 3 m is a common rule).
Lifting and carrying
Back injuries, crushed fingers
Lift with your legs; two people for long lengths and heavy drums; use a trolley.
Trips and slips
Falls over leads, off-cuts and tools
Keep the area tidy, run leads where people do not walk, and sweep up often.
Solvent cement and primer
Fumes, fire, skin and eye irritation
Use in fresh air, keep lids on, no flames or smoking nearby, wear gloves and glasses.
Heat and sun
Heat exhaustion on roofs and open sites
Drink water often, rest in the shade and cover up outdoors.

blocks.note: **You cannot tell asbestos by looking at it.** Many older Jamaican buildings have cement roof sheets, wall panels, water tanks or ceiling boards that may contain it. If your route needs a hole through a material that might be asbestos, stop. Do not drill, cut, sand or break it, and do not 'damp it down' and carry on. Keep people away, report it, and wait until it has been tested and, if needed, dealt with by trained specialists. Your supervisor may agree a route around it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A **risk assessment** is a check, done before the job, of what could cause harm, who could be hurt and how each hazard will be controlled. Your supervisor leads it; you help to spot hazards and you follow the controls. It is reviewed whenever the job or the site changes.

flow: Look at the job and the site
List the hazards
Decide who could be harmed, and how
Choose the controls
Write it down and brief everyone
Review it when anything changes

head: Sign
Meaning
Examples
rows: Blue circle with a white symbol
Mandatory: you **must** do this
Wear eye protection; wear ear protection
Red circle with a red diagonal bar
Prohibition: you must **not** do this
No smoking; do not switch on
Yellow triangle with a black border and symbol
Warning of a hazard
Danger of electric shock (a lightning flash); overhead work
Green rectangle or square
Safe condition
First aid; emergency exit
Red rectangle or square
Fire equipment
Fire extinguisher; fire alarm call point

blocks.p: When your preparation means working on or near an existing circuit, for example opening a box that the new conduit will start from, or chasing a wall beside an old cable, that circuit must be dead. Follow the full procedure every time.

flow: Tell the people affected and agree a time
Identify the circuit from the panel schedule and drawing
Switch off the breaker or isolator
Lock it off with your own padlock and keep the key
Fit a danger tag: 'Do not switch on', your name, the date
Prove your voltage tester on a proving unit
Test at the point of work between every pair of conductors
Prove the tester again on the proving unit
Start work only when the circuit is proved dead

head: Circuit
Test between
rows: 110 V circuit: line, neutral and earth
Line and neutral
Line and earth
Neutral and earth
220 V circuit: two lines and earth, no neutral
Line 1 and line 2
Line 1 and earth
Line 2 and earth
110/220 V circuit: two lines, neutral and earth
Line 1 and line 2
Each line and neutral
Each line and earth
Neutral and earth

blocks.note: A non-contact detector, a neon screwdriver or a lamp cannot prove a circuit dead. Use an approved two-pole voltage tester, checked on a **proving unit** (a small battery device that gives a known voltage) or a known live source before and after the test. If any test shows a voltage, the circuit is not dead: stop and find out why. Only the person who fitted a lock removes it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: If someone is stuck to a live conductor, do not touch them. **Switch off the supply** at the switch, plug or breaker first. If you cannot, stand on something dry and use a dry, non-conducting object, such as a wooden broom handle, to push them or the cable clear. Then call **110** for an ambulance and give first aid as you have been trained.

head: Task
PPE
rows: Every task on a building site
Safety boots with toecaps and sound insulating soles; a hard hat where there is overhead work or the site rules say so
Drilling or chasing block and concrete
Safety glasses or goggles, a dust mask, ear protection and work gloves
Cutting conduit, filing and reaming
Safety glasses; gloves for steel conduit, whose cut edges are sharp
Using solvent cement
Safety glasses, chemical-resistant gloves and fresh air
Working near existing circuits (after isolation)
Cotton or flame-resistant long sleeves, no metal jewellery, insulated tools
Working outdoors in the sun
A hat where a hard hat is not needed, long sleeves and drinking water

blocks.h: Tools for preparing a conduit job

head: Group
Tools
Notes
rows: Measuring and marking
Tape measure, scale rule, spirit level, laser level, plumb bob, chalk line, try square, pencil and marker
A **plumb bob** is a pointed weight on a string that hangs truly vertical. A **chalk line** snaps a long straight line between two marks.
Finding hidden services
Cable and pipe detector
Check it on a known cable first. It can miss deep or screened cables, so still drill with care.
Drilling and fixing
Hammer drill or rotary hammer, masonry and wood bits, screwdrivers, wall plugs and screws
A **hammer drill** hammers as it turns, for drilling block and concrete.
Cutting and bending
Hacksaw, PVC conduit cutter, file, reamer, bending spring, heat gun or hot box for PVC, hand bender for steel tubing
Cut square and remove burrs so that cable insulation is not cut later.
Pulling in (used later, but checked now)
Fish tape (draw tape), draw cord, cable lubricant
A **fish tape** is a long steel or nylon tape pushed through the conduit to pull the cables in.
Testing
Approved two-pole voltage tester and proving unit
Check the leads and probes as well as the tester itself.

head: Tool
Check
rows: Hand tools
Handles tight and not cracked; blades and edges sharp; insulated tools with no cuts, nicks or splits in the insulation
Power tools
Cable, plug and casing undamaged; switch works; guard fitted; the right bit or blade fitted tightly; inspection label in date where the Centre uses them; a 110 V tool only on a 110 V outlet
Battery tools and chargers
Battery not cracked or swollen; charger lead and plug sound
Measuring tools
Tape not kinked and its hook not loose or bent; level vials not cracked; levels and lasers checked against a known line

blocks.p: If you find a fault:

flow: Stop using it
Label it 'DO NOT USE' with the fault, the date and your name
Take it out of use and put it where nobody will pick it up
Report it to your supervisor
Never repair it yourself with tape

ul: For electrical work use a **fibreglass** ladder or steps. Clean, dry fibreglass does not conduct; aluminium does.
Before you climb, check the stiles (rails), rungs or treads, feet, spreaders or locking bars, and labels. Do not use a damaged ladder: tag it and report it.
Open steps fully with the spreaders locked, on firm, level ground. Never stand on the top step or the top cap.
Set a leaning ladder at about **1 m out for every 4 m up**, and tie it or have it footed.
Keep three points of contact and do not over-reach: climb down and move the ladder.
For long spells of work at ceiling height, a work platform or a mobile tower is safer than a ladder.

blocks.p: The drawing and specification say what to use. Your job is to know what each item is for, to check that what arrives is right, and to spot damage before it goes into the building.

head: Conduit
What it is
Use it for
Watch out
rows: Rigid PVC conduit (the type the spec names, for example Schedule 40)
Grey or white plastic tube joined with solvent cement
Most homes and offices; cast in concrete and block; damp places; buildings near the sea

It does not conduct, so a separate earth (equipment grounding) conductor is always run inside. It grows and shrinks with heat and softens if it gets too hot: long runs in the sun need expansion couplings.
Electrical metallic tubing (EMT)
Thin-wall galvanised steel tube with set-screw or compression fittings
Indoor surface runs in dry commercial buildings
Rusts in damp and salty air; set-screw fittings are for dry places only.
Rigid or intermediate metal conduit (RMC, IMC)
Heavy-wall threaded galvanised steel
Workshops, plant rooms and places where conduit could be hit
Heavy and slow to cut and thread; protect cut threads from rust.
Flexible metal conduit
Spiral steel strip
Short final runs to motors and equipment that moves or vibrates
Not for long runs; an earth conductor is usually needed inside it.
Liquid-tight flexible conduit
Flexible conduit with a plastic outer jacket
Short final runs outdoors and in wet or greasy places, such as to an air-conditioning condenser, a pump or an exhaust fan
Use the matching liquid-tight connectors, or the seal is lost.

blocks.note: Salt in the air eats plain steel quickly. For buildings close to the sea, rigid PVC is usually the best choice, with plastic or stainless steel saddles and screws. Where steel conduit must be used near the sea, it should be galvanised and kept painted, as the spec says.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Rigid PVC conduit grows by about **0.05 mm for every metre of length for each 1 °C rise** in temperature, and shrinks by the same amount when it cools. Example: a 10 m run that goes from 25 °C at night to 55 °C in the afternoon sun (a rise of 30 °C) grows by about 10 × 30 × 0.05 = **15 mm**. Fixed tight at both ends, it would bow off the wall or pull its joints apart. An **expansion coupling** takes up the movement; the maker's instructions say where to fit it and how far to set it open.

head: Item
What it does
rows: Coupling
Joins two lengths end to end
Elbow (bend), 90° or 45°
Changes direction; factory elbows give a smooth bend for pulling cables
Male (box) adaptor and locknut
Connects conduit to a box through a knockout
Bush (bushing)
Fitted on the conduit end inside a box to give cables a smooth edge
Outlet and switch boxes; octagon or round ceiling boxes
Hold accessories and light fittings
Junction and draw-in (pull) boxes
Join or pull cables; they must stay accessible
Saddle, strap or clip; spacer saddle
Holds conduit to the surface; a spacer saddle holds it slightly off the wall so that dirt and damp do not collect behind it
Expansion coupling
Lets a long PVC run grow and shrink without buckling
End cap or plug
Closes a conduit end so that concrete, dirt and insects cannot get in during building work
Solvent cement (and primer where the maker asks)
Joins PVC permanently; it must suit the conduit type

blocks.p: All the conduit, fittings and boxes on one run must come from the same system and be the same size. A 3/4 inch fitting from one system may not fit tightly on 3/4 inch conduit from another, and a 20 mm metric fitting will not fit 3/4 inch conduit at all. Loose joints pull apart, let in water and concrete and, on steel conduit, break the earth path.

ul: In conduit, single insulated conductors are usually used (for example the type marked THHN/THWN on US-style wire). The drawing and spec give the type and size.

The designer chooses the size from the **load, the breaker rating, the length of run and the code tables**. Never go by eye or copy the last job. As a guide only: under the NEC, copper 14 AWG is common on 15 A circuits, 12 AWG on 20 A circuits and 10 AWG on 30 A circuits.
The **lower** the AWG number, the **thicker** the wire. Metric cable is sized by its cross-section in mm².

Colours often used in Jamaica: black and red for line (live) conductors, white or grey for neutral, and green, green-and-yellow or bare for earth. Follow the spec, and never trust colours alone on existing wiring.
The code limits how full a conduit may be. Under the NEC, three or more conductors may take up no more than **40%** of the inside area. Use the fill tables, or the drawing, to check the conduit size.

head: Fixing
Use
rows: Plastic wall plug and screw
Light loads in block, concrete and brick. Drill the hole size printed on the packet so that the plug grips.
Hollow-wall anchor or toggle
Hollow block cores, drywall and ceiling boards
Sleeve or wedge anchor
Heavier loads in solid concrete
Self-drilling screw
Thin steel, such as purlins and metal studs

flow: Check items against the materials list and the delivery note
Check type, size, rating and system against the spec
Look for damage: cracked, crushed, bent or sun-faded conduit; broken boxes; damaged cable
Set aside and label wrong or damaged items
Report shortages and damage to your supervisor the same day

blocks.p: A **materials list**, also called a **take-off**, lists every item the job needs, with its size and quantity. Made before the job starts, it means the right items are on site when they are needed, with no wasted trips and no pile of unused stock.

flow: Read the drawing, legend and specification
Count each type of point and box
Measure each run with a scale rule and convert it to a real length
Add the drops down (or up) the walls to each box
Add up the runs, divide by the length of one piece and round up
Count bends, couplings, adaptors, bushes and saddles
Add fixings, solvent cement and cable
Add an allowance for waste
Have the list checked

blocks.p: A drawing at 1:100 shows one ceiling run of 42 mm and another of 63 mm. Each run ends in a drop of 1.5 m down the wall to a box. Conduit comes in 3 m lengths.

head: Step
Working
Result
rows: Run A
Run B
Two drops
Total
Add 10% for waste
Number of 3 m lengths
5 lengths

blocks.p: On a straight run with a saddle at each end: **number of saddles = number of spaces + 1**, where the number of spaces is the length divided by the spacing, rounded up. A 7.5 m run with saddles every 1.5 m has 7.5 ÷ 1.5 = 5 spaces, so it needs **6 saddles**. A 4 m run with saddles every 0.9 m has 4 ÷ 0.9 = 4.4 spaces, rounded up to 5, so it needs 6 saddles.

ul: Add a saddle each side of a bend and close to every box. Under the NEC, PVC conduit is supported within about **0.9 m (3 ft)** of each box, and the small sizes (1/2 to 1 inch) at least every 0.9 m along the run. Steel tubing (EMT) is supported within 0.9 m of each box and at least every 3 m.
Follow the drawing or spec if it asks for closer spacing. Many electricians fix surface conduit closer than the code minimum so that it stays straight in the heat.

blocks.p: For each run: cable = run length × number of conductors, plus an allowance at each box to make the connections (often about 150 to 300 mm per conductor at each end), plus a little spare. Example: a 12 m run carrying a line, a neutral and an earth needs 12 m of **each colour**, plus about 0.3 m of each colour at each of its two boxes: about 12.6 m of each, 37.8 m in all. Order it in the lengths or rolls the supplier sells, by colour.

blocks.note: Always round lengths and pieces **up**, never down: you cannot fix 0.95 of a length you do not have. But do not over-order wildly: a small allowance, often 5 to 10%, covers off-cuts and mistakes. Your supervisor checks the list before it goes to the supplier.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Marking out puts the drawing onto the walls, floors and ceilings. Mark the **whole** route before you cut or fix anything: clashes and mistakes then show up while they cost only a pencil line.

ul: Heights are measured from a **datum**, a fixed reference level. In a finished room this is the **finished floor level (FFL)**. On a site where the floor screed or tiles are not yet down, the builder marks a datum line on the walls, often 1 m above FFL; measure from that line, not from the rough slab.

Take every box height from the drawing or spec. Common heights in Jamaica are about 300 to 450 mm above FFL for ordinary outlets and about 1.2 m for switches, with outlets above kitchen counters set higher, but **the drawing decides**.
Measure every box from the same datum, so that all boxes meant to be at one height line up across the room.
Heights are usually given to the **centre** of a box, or to its bottom: check which on the drawing.

blocks.note: Example: outlets are to be 300 mm above FFL, and the datum line is 1,000 mm above FFL. Measure **down 700 mm** from the datum line to the centre of each box (1,000 − 300 = 700).
blocks.label: Tip

flow: Check positions and heights on the drawing
Mark the centre of each box from the datum
Mark level lines for horizontal runs with a spirit level or laser
Mark plumb lines for drops with a plumb bob or level
Snap chalk lines between the marks
Mark bends, boxes, pull boxes and saddle positions
Scan each fixing point and chase with a detector
Check every mark against the drawing
Ask your supervisor to check before any drilling

head: Tool
Use in marking out
Tip
rows: Spirit level
Short level and plumb lines; checking the tops of boxes
Check it by reading it on a line, turning it end for end on the same line and reading again: a true level reads the same both ways.
Laser level
Long level lines and a datum round a room
Set it on a firm stand and check it against a known mark.
Plumb bob
A true vertical for drops
Let it stop swinging before you mark.
Chalk line
Long straight lines between two marks
Hold it tight, lift it straight out from the wall and snap it once; keep the chalk dry.
Try square
Square marks across a corner or a conduit
Hold the stock firmly against a straight edge.
Tape measure
Positions and spacings
Measure from one fixed point each time, so small errors do not add up.

ul: Use pencil or chalk on surfaces that will be seen: permanent marker can show through paint.
Keep the route clear of corners, door frames and window frames by the distance the drawing or your supervisor gives, so that boxes, saddles and trim all fit.
Mark where the conduit enters and leaves each box, and which knockouts will be used.
Where your route crosses another trade's work, mark it and tell them.
If a mark falls on a hidden service, a beam or a door swing, do not just move it: report it and agree the new position.

sections.title: Working with others, housekeeping and reporting

head: Person
What to agree or tell them
rows: Your supervisor
The latest drawing; the route and any changes; the risk assessment; problems found; when you are ready
The customer or building users

When the power will be off and for how long; which rooms you need and when; furniture to move; what they know about hidden pipes and old wiring; changes they would like, which your supervisor must agree
Other trades: masons, steel fixers, plumbers, carpenters, air-conditioning fitters
Routes on shared walls and ceilings; the order of work (for example conduit in before a slab is poured); who goes first where routes cross

blocks.p: Conduit and water pipes should not be run on top of each other. Agree separate routes, with enough space between them that a leaking pipe cannot drip into a box, and agree who fixes first. Good communication saves time, stops clashes and rework, and keeps people safe, for example when a circuit is switched off.

blocks.note: A slab pour is booked days ahead, with the concrete truck and pump arranged. Your conduit and boxes must be in, tied down, joints sealed, ends capped and checked by your supervisor before then. Missing the pour means cutting into concrete later, which is slow, noisy and can weaken the slab.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Item
How to store it
Why
rows: Conduit lengths
Flat on racks or supports, off the ground, out of the sun, stacked tidily
Stops bending, sagging, sun damage, dirt getting inside and trips
Fittings, boxes and screws
In labelled boxes or bins
Easy to find; nothing lost
Cable drums and reels
Upright on a stand or wedged so they cannot roll; cable ends taped
Stops rolling injuries and damage to cable ends
Solvent cement and primer
Lids closed, in the shade, away from heat, sparks and flames
They are flammable and dry out in the sun
Tools
In a toolbox or locked store; power tools unplugged when not in use
Prevents damage, theft and accidental starting

ul: Sweep up as you go and at the end of every day. Off-cuts, swarf and cable scraps cause trips and slips, and sharp steel off-cuts cut hands and feet.
Put waste in the right bins: PVC off-cuts, steel scrap, cable scrap (which can often be recycled) and general waste. Empty solvent tins go where the site rules say.
Never burn PVC or cable: the smoke is toxic. Never bury waste, and never leave it in a ceiling space.

blocks.h: Reporting at the end of preparation

blocks.p: When preparation is finished, tell your supervisor that the job is ready, and report anything that is not. Your report covers:

ul: The route is marked out and has been checked.
Materials and tools are on site and checked; shortages or damaged items have been reported.
Problems found: clashes, drawing errors, hidden services, possible asbestos, access problems.
Which circuits are isolated and locked off, and who holds the keys.
Changes to the route, marked on the drawing, so that the **as-built drawing** shows where the cables really run.
The job sheet or daily report: hours, materials used and work done.

blocks.note: An as-built drawing that matches the building protects the next electrician. Someone drilling into a wall years from now will trust it.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can read a work order and find the title block, legend, scale, revision and notes on a drawing.
I can explain what a specification tells me and why I must work from the latest revision.
I can recognise common electrical symbols, including S3 for a three-way switch.
I can convert drawing measurements to real lengths at 1:20, 1:50 and 1:100.
I can survey a site for obstacles, hidden services, hazards and access, and record what I find.
I can plan a straight, level route with few bends and pull boxes where the cables need them.
I can take part in a risk assessment and explain the main safety sign colours.
I can carry out safe isolation and name the tests for 110 V and 220 V circuits.
I can say what to do if I find a material that might contain asbestos.
I can choose PPE for drilling, cutting and solvent work, and check tools and ladders before use.
I can choose between PVC, EMT, rigid steel and flexible conduit for a given place, and name the main fittings.
I can explain why one conduit system and size is used on a run, and why PVC needs expansion couplings in the sun.
I can work out conduit lengths, saddles and cable for a materials list, rounding up and allowing for waste.
I can mark out box positions from a datum, and level and plumb lines with the right tools.
I can agree routes and timing with my supervisor, the customer and other trades.
I can store materials properly, keep the site tidy and dispose of waste correctly.
I can report that a job is ready, and record route changes for the as-built drawing.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: 110 V and 220 V, 50 Hz
The supply to most Jamaican homes; lighting is usually 110 V
Common drawing scales: multiply a drawing measurement by 50 or 100
360° (four quarter bends)
The most bending allowed between pull points under the NEC
The most of a conduit's inside area that three or more conductors may fill under the NEC
About 0.9 m
NEC support spacing for small PVC conduit, and the distance from a box to the nearest support
About 0.05 mm per metre per °C
How much rigid PVC conduit grows as it warms
Spaces + 1
Saddles on a straight run with one at each end
1 in 4
Leaning ladder: 1 m out for every 4 m up

terms: A drawing marked up to show what was actually installed, including any changes to the planned route.
A fitting on a conduit end inside a box that gives the cables a smooth edge.
A fixed reference level from which heights are measured, such as the finished floor level or a line marked on the wall.
An accessible box on a conduit run where cables can be pulled through without strain.
A drawing of one wall or side of a building, showing heights.
A fitting that lets a PVC conduit run grow and shrink with temperature.
The level of the floor once the tiles or screed are laid.
A long steel or nylon tape pushed through conduit to pull cables in.
The list on a drawing that says what each symbol means.
A list of every item a job needs, with sizes and quantities, worked out from the drawing.
A small device that gives a known voltage, used to show a voltage tester is working.
A numbered or lettered version of a drawing; only the latest one is used.
A check of what could cause harm on a job and how each hazard will be controlled.
A clip that holds conduit firmly to a surface.
The ratio between a drawing and the real building, such as 1:50.
The document that sets out the materials, standard of work, code and tests for a job.
The box on a drawing that gives its title, number, scale, date and who drew it.

c1.title: Rough-in at a new house in Old Harbour
c1.text: Romaine Ellis, a Level 2 trainee, is working with electrician Mr Lloyd Campbell on a new three-bedroom block-and-concrete house in Old Harbour, St Catherine. The roof slab is to be poured on Thursday, and the ceiling conduits and boxes must be in before then. The layout drawing is at a scale of 1:100. The copy in the van is revision A, but the site office has revision B. The floor screed is not yet laid; the builder has marked a datum line on the walls 1,000 mm above finished floor level.

c2.title: Extra circuits in a Morant Bay clinic
c2.text: Trainee Tevin Morgan and electrician Mrs Sonia Whyte are preparing to extend two circuits in a health clinic in Morant Bay, St Thomas, which stays open while they work. The new route starts from an existing outlet box on circuit 7 and passes through an old store room lined with grey cement wall sheets. The panel schedule says circuit 7 feeds 'store room outlets', but the clinic's vaccine fridge is plugged into an outlet on the same wall. Part of the route must be chased into a block wall beside the waiting area.

c3.title: A beach restaurant in Negril
c3.text: Trainee Shamar Reid and his supervisor Mr Errol Brown are preparing the wiring for a new open-sided restaurant about 20 m from the sea in Negril, Westmoreland. The specification calls for rigid PVC conduit on the surface. One straight run is 18 m long, along a beam that gets the full afternoon sun. A kitchen exhaust fan will be mounted on a vibrating frame. The supplier has delivered EMT steel tubing with set-screw fittings instead of PVC.

c4.title: A classroom block in Santa Cruz
c4.text: Trainee Kerry-Ann Thompson and electrician Mr Delroy Gayle are marking out surface PVC conduit in a new classroom at a high school in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. The floors are finished. The main run is 7.2 m long along the back wall, with saddles at 0.9 m centres and one at each end. Two drops of 1.8 m each go down from that run to switch boxes. Conduit comes in 3 m lengths.

c5.title: Low-level runs in an Ewarton furniture workshop
c5.text: Trainee Andre Walters and electrician Ms Marcia Edwards are preparing surface conduit runs in a furniture workshop in Ewarton, St Catherine. Trolleys of timber are pushed along the walls all day, and the specification calls for galvanised steel conduit at low level. Some marking out must be done at about 3 m. The store has an aluminium extension ladder and a fibreglass stepladder whose spreader lock is broken.

questions.q: Romaine notices that the van's drawing is revision A while the site office has revision B. What should he do before any conduit goes on the slab steel?
o: Use revision A, since revision changes are usually small details
Use revision A for the slab and revision B later for the walls
Get revision B and check every route and box position against it
Ask the mason which revision he has been building the walls to
questions.why: Only the latest revision shows what the designer wants now; an older copy may have points moved, added or removed. Conduit cast in the wrong place is very costly to correct, so every route and box is checked against revision B.

questions.q: On revision B, the ceiling run from the panel to the living-room light is 57 mm long on paper. What length is that run on site?
questions.why: At 1:100, multiply by 100: 57 mm × 100 = 5,700 mm = 5.7 m. A useful check is that 1 cm on a 1:100 drawing is 1 m on site, so 5.7 cm is 5.7 m.

questions.q: The drawing shows 'S3' beside a switch at each end of the passage. What does this tell Romaine?
o: The switch is on circuit number 3 at the panel
The switch is mounted 3 feet above the floor
Three separate switches share one box
Two switches control one light from two places
questions.why: On US-style drawings, S3 means a three-way switch (called a two-way switch in British terms). A pair of them controls one light from two places, so the conduit and cable between them must allow for the extra conductors. Always confirm with the legend.

questions.q: Outlet boxes are to be 300 mm above finished floor level. How should Romaine set their height on the walls of this house?
o: Up 300 mm from the rough slab
Down 700 mm from the datum line
Down 300 mm from the datum line
Up 300 mm from the datum line
questions.why: The screed is not laid yet, so the rough slab is the wrong reference. The datum line is 1,000 mm above finished floor level, so a box 300 mm above FFL is 1,000 − 300 = 700 mm below the datum line.

questions.q: What must be done to the ceiling conduits before Thursday's pour?
o: Leave the ends open so the cables can be pushed in after the pour
Tie them to the steel, seal joints, cap ends and get them checked
Lay them loose on the formwork so the concrete can settle them
Wrap each joint in masking tape and rely on the wet concrete to hold it
questions.why: Wet concrete moves loose conduit and gets into open ends and joints, leaving blocked runs that cannot be used. Tied, sealed and capped conduit, checked by the supervisor before the pour, avoids cutting into a finished slab later.

questions.q: Before isolating circuit 7, Tevin sees the vaccine fridge plugged in on the same wall as the store room outlets. What should he do?
o: Switch off quickly, since the fridge will stay cold for a short while
Trust the panel schedule, because an electrician must have written it
Switch circuit 7 off and watch whether the fridge light goes out
Check which circuit feeds the fridge and agree a plan with the clinic
questions.why: Schedules are often wrong or out of date, and losing power to a vaccine fridge could spoil the vaccines. Tevin and Mrs Whyte find out which circuit feeds it and agree with the clinic how it will stay powered before anything is switched off.

questions.q: The clinic administrator looks at the grey cement sheets and says, 'They look fine, just drill through.' What is the right reply?
o: Nobody can tell asbestos by eye, so leave them until tested
Drill through, as long as everybody nearby wears a dust mask
Drill through, but wet the sheets first to hold the dust down
Drill slowly, because slow drilling does not release any fibres
questions.why: Old cement sheets may contain asbestos, and nobody can tell by looking. Drilling them can release fibres that cause deadly lung disease years later, and masks or water do not make it safe. Leave them alone, report them, and let the supervisor arrange a test or a route around them.

questions.q: Circuit 7 is locked off and tagged and the tester has been proved. At the outlet box the tester shows 110 V between line and earth, and nothing between line and neutral. What should Tevin conclude?
o: The tester is faulty, so he checks again with a neon screwdriver
Line to neutral shows nothing, so the outlet box is safe to work on
The box is still live from some source, so he stops and finds out why
This is a normal stray reading on a circuit that has been switched off
questions.why: Any voltage between any pair of conductors means the circuit is not dead. The box may be fed from another circuit, or the neutral may be broken or wrongly connected. Stop, keep clear and trace the cause with the supervisor before any work.

questions.q: Tevin must chase a short run into the block wall next to the waiting area. Which plan controls the dust best?
o: Wet the wall first, then chase it without a mask as the dust is damp
Wear a dust mask himself and leave the waiting area open as usual
Chase quickly at lunchtime so the dust settles before patients return
Use a chaser with dust extraction, screen the area and wear a mask
questions.why: Chasing block makes fine dust that harms the lungs of anyone nearby, not only the person cutting. Extraction removes most of it at the source, a screen keeps patients away, and a suitable dust mask protects Tevin.

questions.q: What should Shamar do with the EMT and set-screw fittings that were delivered in place of PVC?
o: Use them, since steel protects the cables better than PVC
Set them aside, label them and report the wrong delivery
Use them, but paint every set-screw joint once it is fixed
Use them on the sunny beam and PVC everywhere else
questions.why: The specification calls for rigid PVC, and thin-wall steel with set-screw fittings rusts quickly in salty sea air and is meant for dry places. Wrong deliveries are checked against the spec, set aside, labelled and reported, not used.

questions.q: Why does the 18 m run along the sunny beam need expansion couplings?
o: The PVC grows and shrinks with heat and could bow or pull apart
They let the run be joined without using any solvent cement
They let rainwater drain out of the conduit after a heavy storm
They let a bigger cable be pulled into the run at a later date
questions.why: Rigid PVC grows about 0.05 mm per metre for each °C. An 18 m run heated by 30 °C grows about 27 mm. Fixed tight with no expansion coupling, it bows off the beam or pulls its joints open.

questions.q: What is the best choice for the final short connection to the kitchen exhaust fan?
o: Rigid PVC conduit with an extra 90° bend close to the fan
EMT tubing fixed rigidly to the steel frame that holds the fan
Liquid-tight flexible conduit and its own connectors
Cable with no conduit at all, tied to the fan's bracket
questions.why: The fan vibrates, so a rigid connection would crack or work loose, and a kitchen is greasy and damp. Liquid-tight flexible conduit absorbs the movement and keeps out water and grease, as long as its own connectors are used.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann will fix the 7.2 m back-wall run with a saddle at each end and the rest at 0.9 m centres. What total does she need for that run?
questions.why: 7.2 ÷ 0.9 = 8 spaces. With a saddle at each end there is always one more saddle than spaces, so 8 + 1 = 9.

questions.q: She reads her spirit level on a line, turns it end for end on the same line, and the bubble now reads differently. What does this show?
o: The level is out of true and must not be used for marking
The wall is out of plumb, so she must mark the line by eye
The bubble reads differently in hot weather, which is normal
The line is level, because the bubble moved when she turned it
questions.why: A true level reads the same both ways round on the same line. If the reading changes, the level itself is wrong, and every line marked with it would be out. Report it and use a level that passes the check.

questions.q: The materials for this job are the 7.2 m run and the two 1.8 m drops. With 10% added for waste, how many 3 m lengths of conduit should she order?
questions.why: 7.2 + 1.8 + 1.8 = 10.8 m. Adding 10% gives 10.8 × 1.1 = 11.88 m. 11.88 ÷ 3 = 3.96, which rounds up to 4 lengths.

questions.q: Before drilling for the saddles, Kerry-Ann scans the wall with a cable detector and gets no signal. Why should she still take care when drilling?
o: The detector only works when every circuit is switched on
A detector finds metal pipes but never finds any cables
The detector should be used after the holes are drilled
Detectors can miss deep or screened cables and some pipes
questions.why: A detector is a useful check but not a guarantee. Cables deep in a wall, screened cables and plastic pipes may not show. Check the drawings, think about where services usually run, and drill steadily to the marked depth.

questions.q: Why does the specification call for galvanised steel conduit at low level in this workshop?
o: Steel stands up to knocks from trolleys and timber much better
Steel conduit needs no earth conductor anywhere in the building
Steel conduit is lighter and quicker to fix than PVC conduit
PVC conduit is not allowed in any building that has machines
questions.why: Where conduit could be hit, strong steel conduit protects the cables. It is heavier and slower to work than PVC, and an earth path must still be provided, but it will not crack when a loaded trolley hits it.

questions.q: Andre needs to reach about 3 m to mark out a ceiling run. Which way of getting up there is right?
o: Use the aluminium ladder, as it is the only one that is undamaged
Use the stepladder carefully, holding the broken spreader closed
Stand on the workshop bench, which is wide and steady enough
Report the steps and use a sound fibreglass ladder or platform
questions.why: Aluminium conducts, so it is the wrong choice for electrical work, and a stepladder with a broken spreader lock can collapse. The damaged steps are tagged and reported, and a sound fibreglass ladder or a work platform is used.

questions.q: Under the NEC, how much bending may a conduit run have between two pull points?
o: Two quarter bends, 180° in all
Three quarter bends, 270° in all
Four quarter bends, 360° in all
Six quarter bends, 540° in all
questions.why: Every bend adds friction when cables are pulled in. The NEC limits a run between pull points to the equivalent of four quarter bends (360°). Beyond that, a pull box is needed so cables are not strained or damaged.

questions.q: Which safety sign tells you that something is forbidden, such as 'Do not switch on'?
o: A blue circle with a white symbol
A red circle with a diagonal bar
A yellow triangle with a black edge
A green square with a white symbol
questions.why: Red circles with a bar are prohibition signs. Blue circles are mandatory (you must), yellow triangles warn of a hazard, and green signs show safe conditions such as first aid and exits.
